claim: The interaction between the SARS-CoV-2 virus Spike protein receptor binding domain (RBD) and the ACE2 cell surface protein is required for viral infection of cells.
source: The interaction between the SARS-CoV-2 virus Spike protein receptor binding domain (RBD) and the ACE2 cell surface protein is required for viral infection of cells.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about SARS-CoV-2 infection mechanism.

claim: Mutations in the RBD are present in SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern that have emerged independently worldwide.
source: Mutations in the RBD are present in SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern that have emerged independently worldwide.
evidence: This is supported by epidemiological data and variant surveillance.

claim: The B.1.1.7 lineage has a mutation (N501Y) in its Spike RBD that enhances binding to ACE2.
source: For example, the B.1.1.7 lineage has a mutation (N501Y) in its Spike RBD that enhances binding to ACE2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing increased affinity.

claim: Most of the RBD mutations studied (N501Y, E484K, and S477N) increased the affinity of the RBD/ACE2 interaction.
source: Most of these mutations increased the affinity of the RBD/ACE2 interaction.
evidence: This is directly supported by the SPR measurements presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: The K417N/T mutations decreased the affinity of the RBD/ACE2 interaction.
source: The exceptions were mutations K417N/T, which decreased the affinity.
evidence: This is directly supported by the SPR measurements presented in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: The N501Y and S477N mutations enhance transmission primarily by enhancing binding.
source: Taken together with other studies, our results suggest that the N501Y and S477N mutations enhance transmission primarily by enhancing binding, the K417N/T mutations facilitate immune escape, and the E484K mutation enhances binding and immune escape.
evidence: This is based on the experimental data from this study combined with inference from cited literature.

claim: The K417N/T mutations facilitate immune escape.
source: Taken together with other studies, our results suggest that the N501Y and S477N mutations enhance transmission primarily by enhancing binding, the K417N/T mutations facilitate immune escape, and the E484K mutation enhances binding and immune escape.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing decreased affinity combined with citations about immune escape.

claim: The E484K mutation enhances binding and immune escape.
source: Taken together with other studies, our results suggest that the N501Y and S477N mutations enhance transmission primarily by enhancing binding, the K417N/T mutations facilitate immune escape, and the E484K mutation enhances binding and immune escape.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing increased affinity combined with citations about immune escape.

claim: More than 135 million people have been infected with SARS-CoV-2, resulting in the deaths of more than 3 million people.
source: To date, more than 135 million people have been infected, resulting in the deaths from the resulting disease, COVID-19, of more than 3 million people (WHO, 2021), and measures introduced to control spread have had harmful social and economic impacts.
evidence: This is cited from WHO data.

claim: Effective vaccines have been developed for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Fortunately, effective vaccines have been developed, and a global vaccination programme is underway (Mahase, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: New SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern are emerging that may increase transmissibility of the virus.
source: New SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern are emerging that are making containment of the pandemic more difficult, perhaps by increasing transmissibility of the virus (Davies et al., 2021; Korber et al., 2020; Volz et al., 2021b; Volz et al., 2021b; Washington et al., 2021) and/or its resistance to protective immunity induced by previous infection or vaccines (Darby and Hiscox, 2021; Dejnirattisai et al., 2021; Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Madhi et al., 2021a; Madhi et al., 2021b; Mahase, 2021; Volz et al., 2021b; Volz et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: New SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern may have increased resistance to protective immunity induced by previous infection or vaccines.
source: New SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern are emerging that are making containment of the pandemic more difficult, perhaps by increasing transmissibility of the virus (Davies et al., 2021; Korber et al., 2020; Volz et al., 2021b; Volz et al., 2021b; Washington et al., 2021) and/or its resistance to protective immunity induced by previous infection or vaccines (Darby and Hiscox, 2021; Dejnirattisai et al., 2021; Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Madhi et al., 2021a; Madhi et al., 2021b; Mahase, 2021; Volz et al., 2021b; Volz et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published studies.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 virus enters cells following an interaction between the Spike (S) protein on its surface with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) on cell surfaces.
source: The SARS-CoV-2 virus enters cells following an interaction between the Spike (S) protein on its surface with angiotensin-converting enzyme 2 (ACE2) on cell surfaces (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from literature.

claim: The receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the Spike protein binds the membrane-distal portion of the ACE2 protein.
source: The receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the Spike protein binds the membrane-distal portion of the ACE2 protein.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge.

claim: The S protein forms a homotrimer, which is cleaved shortly after synthesis into two fragments that remain associated non-covalently: S1, which contains the RBD, and S2, which mediates membrane fusion following the binding of Spike to ACE2.
source: The S protein forms a homotrimer, which is cleaved shortly after synthesis into two fragments that remain associated non-covalently: S1, which contains the RBD, and S2, which mediates membrane fusion following the binding of Spike to ACE2 (V'kovski et al., 2021).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from literature.

claim: The D614G mutation emerged early in Europe and quickly became dominant globally.
source: One that emerged early in Europe, D614G, and quickly became dominant globally (Korber et al., 2020), increases the density of intact Spike trimer on the virus surface by preventing premature dissociation of S1 from S2 following cleavage (Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The D614G mutation increases the density of intact Spike trimer on the virus surface by preventing premature dissociation of S1 from S2 following cleavage.
source: One that emerged early in Europe, D614G, and quickly became dominant globally (Korber et al., 2020), increases the density of intact Spike trimer on the virus surface by preventing premature dissociation of S1 from S2 following cleavage (Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The N501Y mutation lies within the RBD and increases its affinity for ACE2.
source: A later mutation, N501Y, which has appeared in multiple lineages, lies within the RBD, and increases its affinity for ACE2 (Starr et al., 2020; Supasa et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations and the experimental data in this manuscript.

claim: Mutations that directly or indirectly enhance Spike binding to ACE2 may increase transmissibility.
source: These findings suggest that mutations that directly or indirectly enhance Spike binding to ACE2 may increase transmissibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and cited literature.

claim: Prior infection by SARS-CoV-2 and current vaccines induce antibody responses to the Spike protein.
source: Prior infection by SARS-CoV-2 and current vaccines induce antibody responses to the Spike protein, and most neutralising antibodies appear to bind to the Spike RBD (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Greaney et al., 2021a; Rogers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Most neutralising antibodies appear to bind to the Spike RBD.
source: Prior infection by SARS-CoV-2 and current vaccines induce antibody responses to the Spike protein, and most neutralising antibodies appear to bind to the Spike RBD (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Greaney et al., 2021a; Rogers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Some variants of concern have mutations in their RBD that confer resistance to neutralising antibodies.
source: Some variants of concern have mutations in their RBD that confer resistance to neutralising antibodies (Darby and Hiscox, 2021; Dejnirattisai et al., 2021; Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Madhi et al., 2021a; Madhi et al., 2021b; Mahase, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Previous studies of the interaction between the Spike RBD and ACE2 have produced a wide range of affinity and kinetic estimates under conditions that are not always well defined.
source: Previous studies of the interaction between the Spike RBD and ACE2 have produced a wide range of affinity and kinetic estimates under conditions (e.g. temperature) that are not always well defined (Lei et al., 2020; Shang et al., 2020; Supasa et al., 2021; Wrapp et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is based on citations to previous studies.

claim: The study measured the interaction between Spike RBD and ACE2 at a physiological temperature (37°C).
source: In this study, we undertook a detailed affinity and kinetic analysis of the interaction between Spike RBD and ACE2 at a physiological temperature (37°C), taking care to avoid common pitfalls.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental conditions.

claim: Both mutations of ACE2 (S19P, K26R) enhanced the interaction with RBD.
source: Both mutations of ACE2 (S19P, K26R) and most of the mutations of RBD (N501Y, E484K, and S477N) enhanced the interaction, with one RBD mutation (N501Y) increasing the affinity by ~10-fold.
evidence: This is directly supported by the SPR measurements in Table 1 and Figure 4.

claim: The N501Y mutation increased the affinity by ~10-fold.
source: Both mutations of ACE2 (S19P, K26R) and most of the mutations of RBD (N501Y, E484K, and S477N) enhanced the interaction, with one RBD mutation (N501Y) increasing the affinity by ~10-fold.
evidence: This is directly supported by the SPR measurements in Table 1.

claim: Increased binding was the result of decreases in dissociation rate constants (N501Y, S477N) and/or increases in association rate constants (N501Y, E484K).
source: Increased binding was the result of decreases in dissociation rate constants (N501Y, S477N) and/or increases in association rate constants (N501Y, E484K).
evidence: This is directly supported by the kinetic measurements in Table 1.

claim: The affinity-enhancing N501Y and E484K mutations that are present in both Beta and Gamma variants confer a net ~4-fold increase in the affinity of their RBDs for ACE2.
source: Although the K417N/T mutations found in the South African (B.1.351) and Brazilian (P.1) variants both decreased the affinity, the affinity-enhancing N501Y and E484K mutations that are also present in both variants confer a net ~4-fold increase in the affinity of their RBDs for ACE2.
evidence: This is calculated from the experimental data in Table 1.

claim: The N501Y mutation has appeared in the Alpha (B.1.1.7), Beta (B.1.351), and Gamma (P.1) variants.
source: The N501Y mutation has appeared in the Alpha (B.1.1.7; 20I/501Y.V1), Beta (B.1.351; 20 H/501Y.V2), and Gamma (P.1; 20 J/501Y.V3) variants, which were first identified in the UK, South Africa, and Brazil, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The E484K mutation is present in the Beta and Gamma variants and has appeared independently in many other lineages.
source: The E484K mutation is present in the Beta and Gamma variants and has appeared independently in many other lineages, including Zeta (P.2; 20B/S.484K), B.1.1.318, Eta (B.1.525; 20A/S:484 K), and Iota (B.1.526; 20 C/S.484K).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: E484K has appeared in VOC-202102–02, a subset of the Alpha variant identified in the UK.
source: E484K has also appeared in VOC-202102–02, a subset of the Alpha variant identified in the UK (SARS-CoV-2 Variants of concern and variants under investigation - GOV.UK, 2021).
evidence: This is cited from a government report.

claim: The S477N mutation became dominant for periods in Australia (clade 20 F) and parts of Europe (20A.EU2) and then appeared in New York in the Iota or B.1.526 lineage.
source: The S477N mutation became dominant for periods in Australia (clade 20 F) and parts of Europe (20A.EU2) and then appeared in New York in the Iota or B.1.526 lineage (Zhou et al., 2021a).
evidence: This is cited from literature and supported by Figure 1.

claim: Mutations of K417 have appeared independently in the Beta and Gamma variants.
source: Mutations of K417 have appeared independently in the Beta and Gamma variants.
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: N501Y, E484K, and S477N were the main mutations that appeared following random RBD mutagenesis and in vitro selection of mutants with enhanced ACE2 binding.
source: Interestingly, N501Y, E484K, and S477N were the main mutations that appeared following random RBD mutagenesis and in vitro selection of mutants with enhanced ACE2 binding (Zahradník et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: K26R is the most common ACE2 mutation within the RBD binding site, present in 0.4% of all samples in the gnomAD database.
source: They are present in 0.4% and 0.03%, respectively, of all samples in the gnomAD database (Karczewski et al., 2020), while other ACE2 mutations in the RBD binding site are much less frequent (<0.004%) (MacGowan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from the gnomAD database.

claim: S19P is present in 0.03% of all samples in the gnomAD database.
source: They are present in 0.4% and 0.03%, respectively, of all samples in the gnomAD database (Karczewski et al., 2020), while other ACE2 mutations in the RBD binding site are much less frequent (<0.004%) (MacGowan et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from the gnomAD database.

claim: K26R is most common in Ashkenazi Jews (1%) and (non-Finnish) north-western Europeans (0.6%).
source: K26R is observed in all the major gnomAD populations but is most common in Ashkenazi Jews (1%) and (non-Finnish) north-western Europeans (0.6%).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the gnomAD database.

claim: K26R is less common in Africans/African-Americans and South Asians (0.1%) and rare in Finnish (0.05%) and East-Asian (0.001%) populations.
source: It is less common in Africans/African-Americans and South Asians (0.1%) and rare in Finnish (0.05%) and East-Asian (0.001%) populations.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the gnomAD database.

claim: The S19P mutant is almost exclusively found in Africans/African-Americans (0.3%).
source: The S19P mutant is almost exclusively found in Africans/African-Americans (0.3%).
evidence: This is based on analysis of the gnomAD database.

claim: The measured association rate constant (kon) for WT RBD binding to WT ACE2 was 0.9 ± 0.05 μM–1s–1.
source: Excellent fits of 1:1 Langmuir binding model to the data yielded an association rate constant (kon) of 0.9 ± 0.05 μM–1s–1 and a dissociation rate constant (koff) of 0.067 ± 0.0011 s–1 (mean ± SD, n = 6, Table 1).
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The measured dissociation rate constant (koff) for WT RBD binding to WT ACE2 was 0.067 ± 0.0011 s–1.
source: Excellent fits of 1:1 Langmuir binding model to the data yielded an association rate constant (kon) of 0.9 ± 0.05 μM–1s–1 and a dissociation rate constant (koff) of 0.067 ± 0.0011 s–1 (mean ± SD, n = 6, Table 1).
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The measured rate constants are up to 25-fold faster than previously reported for the same interaction.
source: These rate constants are up to 25- fold faster than previously reported for the same interaction (Lei et al., 2020; Shang et al., 2020; Supasa et al., 2021; Wrapp et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature.

claim: Previous experiments were conducted at unphysiologically low temperatures (i.e. below 37°C).
source: However, previous experiments were conducted at unphysiologically low temperatures (i.e. below 37°C) and under conditions in which mass-transport limitations and rebinding are highly likely (see Discussion).
evidence: This is inferred from analysis of cited literature.

claim: The calculated dissociation constant (KD) for WT RBD binding to WT ACE2 was 74 ± 4 nM.
source: The calculated dissociation constant (KD) was 74 ± 4 nM (mean ± SD, n = 6, Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated from the measured kinetic data in Table 1.

claim: The equilibrium KD measured for WT RBD binding to WT ACE2 was 63 ± 7.7 nM.
source: This KD was very similar to the value calculated from kinetic data (63 ± 7.7 nM [mean ± SD, n = 24, Table 1]), and did not vary with immobilisation level (Figure 2E), further validating our kinetic measurements.
evidence: This is directly measured by equilibrium binding as shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: The affinity values measured are within the wide range reported in previous studies, which varied from KD 6–133 nM.
source: These affinity values are within the wide range reported in previous studies, which varied from KD 6–133 nM (Laffeber et al., 2021; Lei et al., 2020; Liu et al., 2021; Shang et al., 2020; Supasa et al., 2021; Wrapp et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature.

claim: The S477N mutation increased the affinity ~1.5-fold by decreasing the koff.
source: The S477N and E484K mutations increased the affinity more modestly (~1.5-fold), by decreasing the koff (S477N) or increasing the kon (E484K).
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The E484K mutation increased the affinity ~1.5-fold by increasing the kon.
source: The S477N and E484K mutations increased the affinity more modestly (~1.5-fold), by decreasing the koff (S477N) or increasing the kon (E484K).
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The K417T mutation decreased the affinity ~2-fold, mainly by decreasing the kon but also by increasing the koff.
source: The K417T and K417N mutations decreased the affinity ~2- and ~ 4-fold, respectively, mainly by decreasing the kon but also by increasing the koff.
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The K417N mutation decreased the affinity ~4-fold, mainly by decreasing the kon but also by increasing the koff.
source: The K417T and K417N mutations decreased the affinity ~2- and ~ 4-fold, respectively, mainly by decreasing the kon but also by increasing the koff.
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: K417 forms a salt bridge with D30 on ACE2.
source: K417 forms a salt bridge with D30 on ACE2 (Lan et al., 2020), while E484 is ~9 Å from E75 on ACE2 (Lan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from structural data.

claim: E484 is ~9 Å from E75 on ACE2.
source: K417 forms a salt bridge with D30 on ACE2 (Lan et al., 2020), while E484 is ~9 Å from E75 on ACE2 (Lan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from structural data.

claim: The mutations K417N/T and E484K would decrease and increase, respectively, long-range electrostatic forces that may accelerate association.
source: Thus, the mutations K417N/T and E484K would decrease and increase, respectively, long-range electrostatic forces that may accelerate association (Schreiber and Fersht, 1996).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and cited literature on electrostatic interactions.

claim: The addition of the E484K mutation to N501Y further increased the affinity, to ~15-fold higher than WT RBD (KD ~5 nM), by further increasing the kon.
source: In the case of VOC-202102–02, the addition of the E484K mutation to N501Y further increased the affinity, to ~15-fold higher than WT RBD (KD ~5 nM), by further increasing the kon.
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The affinity of the Beta (K417N/ E484K/N501Y) variant for ACE2 increased by 3.7-fold relative to wild-type RBD, by both increasing the kon and decreasing the koff rate constants.
source: The affinity of the Beta (K417N/ E484K/N501Y) and Gamma (K417T/E484K/N501Y) RBD variants for ACE2 increased by 3.7- and 5.3-fold, respectively, relative to wild-type RBD, by both increasing the kon and decreasing the koff rate constants.
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The affinity of the Gamma (K417T/E484K/N501Y) variant for ACE2 increased by 5.3-fold relative to wild-type RBD, by both increasing the kon and decreasing the koff rate constants.
source: The affinity of the Beta (K417N/ E484K/N501Y) and Gamma (K417T/E484K/N501Y) RBD variants for ACE2 increased by 3.7- and 5.3-fold, respectively, relative to wild-type RBD, by both increasing the kon and decreasing the koff rate constants.
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 3 and Table 1.

claim: The effects of multiple mutations on binding affinity are additive.
source: We next examined whether the effects of the mutations were additive, as is typically the case for multiple mutations at protein/protein interfaces (Wells, 1990).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3D and cited literature.

claim: The ΔΔG measured for RBD variants with multiple mutations was equal to the sum of the ΔΔG values measured for the individual RBD mutants.
source: This was indeed the case (Figure 3D), indicating that the effects on each mutation are independent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 3D.

claim: The effects of each mutation are independent.
source: This was indeed the case (Figure 3D), indicating that the effects on each mutation are independent. This is consistent with them being spaced well apart within the interface (Figure 1C) and validates the accuracy of the affinity measurements.
evidence: This is inferred from the additive effects shown in Figure 3D and the structural data in Figure 1C.

claim: The S19P ACE2 mutation increased the affinity of WT RBD binding by ~3.7-fold.
source: Both S19P and K26R increased the affinity of WT RBD binding by ~3.7- and ~ 2.4-fold (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The K26R ACE2 mutation increased the affinity of WT RBD binding by ~2.4-fold.
source: Both S19P and K26R increased the affinity of WT RBD binding by ~3.7- and ~ 2.4-fold (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: The increases in affinity from ACE2 mutations were the result of both increases in the kon and decreases in the koff.
source: These increases in affinity were the result of both increases in the kon and decreases in the koff.
evidence: This is directly measured by SPR as shown in Figure 4 and Table 1.

claim: In most cases, the effects of ACE2 and RBD mutations were largely independent.
source: In most cases, ΔΔΔG values were close to zero, indicating that the effects of these mutations were largely independent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 4B,C.

claim: The combination of ACE2 S19P and RBD S477N variants showed non-independent effects.
source: The one exception was the combination of ACE2 S19P and RBD S477N variants, where the measured value was significantly lower than the predicted value (Figure 4B), indicating that these mutations were not independent.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 4B.

claim: The ACE2 residue S19 is adjacent to RBD residue S477 in the contact interface.
source: This is consistent with the fact that the ACE2 residue S19 is adjacent to RBD residue S477 in the contact interface (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in the structural data in Figure 1C.

claim: The S477N mutation increased the affinity of RBD for ACE2 WT but decreased its affinity for ACE2 S19P.
source: An important consequence of this is that the S477N mutation increased the affinity of RBD for ACE2 WT but decreased its affinity for ACE2 S19P.
evidence: This is inferred from the data in Table 1 and Figure 4.

claim: One likely reason for faster rate constants measured in this study compared to previous reports is that previous measurements were performed at a lower temperature.
source: One likely reason for this is that previous measurements were performed at a lower temperature, which almost always decreases rate constants.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with cited literature and general knowledge about temperature effects on kinetics.

claim: A second likely reason for faster rate constants is that previous kinetic studies were performed under conditions in which the rate of diffusion of soluble molecule to the sensor surface limits the association rate, and rebinding of dissociated molecules to the surface reduces the measured dissociation rate.
source: A second likely reason is that previous kinetic studies were performed under conditions in which the rate of diffusion of soluble molecule to the sensor surface limits the association rate, and rebinding of dissociated molecules to the surface reduces the measured dissociation rate.
evidence: This is inferred from comparison with cited literature and knowledge of SPR artifacts.

claim: Mass-transport limitations and rebinding are known pitfalls of surface plasmon resonance and bilayer interferometry.
source: These are known pitfalls of both techniques used in these studies, surface plasmon resonance (Myszka, 1997), and bilayer interferometry (Abdiche et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from methodological literature.

claim: The present study avoided mass-transport limitations and rebinding by immobilising a very low level of ligand on the sensor surface.
source: In the present study, we avoided these issues by immobilising a very low level of ligand on the sensor surface.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the experimental design.

claim: Protein aggregates can cause problems even when aggregates are a very minor contaminant.
source: A third possible reason is that the proteins were aggregated, which can cause problems even when aggregates are a very minor contaminant (van der Merwe and Barclay, 1996).
evidence: This is cited from methodological literature.

claim: The presence of aggregates can be excluded if the simple 1:1 Langmuir binding model fits the kinetic data.
source: The presence of aggregates results in complex binding kinetics, which can be excluded if the simple 1:1 Langmuir binding model fits the kinetic data.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of binding kinetics and cited literature.

claim: The RBD mutations selected for analysis have all emerged independently and became dominant in a region at least once in different lineages.
source: The RBD mutations that we selected for analysis have all emerged independently and became dominant in a region at least once in different lineages, suggesting that they provide a selective advantage.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological data and phylogenetic analysis.

claim: The RBD mutations selected for analysis provide a selective advantage.
source: The RBD mutations that we selected for analysis have all emerged independently and became dominant in a region at least once in different lineages, suggesting that they provide a selective advantage.
evidence: This is inferred from the epidemiological patterns.

claim: Epidemiological studies have suggested that the Alpha variant has enhanced transmissibility.
source: Second, epidemiological studies have suggested that the Alpha variant, which has the N501Y mutation, has enhanced transmissibility (Volz et al., 2021a; Washington et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from epidemiological studies.

claim: A SARS-CoV-2 variant with the Spike mutation D614G rapidly became dominant globally after it emerged.
source: Finally, a SARS-CoV-2 variant with the Spike mutation D614G, which increases its activity by stabilising it following furin cleavage (Zhang et al., 2021; Zhang et al., 2020), rapidly became dominant globally after it emerged (Korber et al., 2020; Volz et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is cited from epidemiological studies.

claim: The WT Spike/ACE2 interaction is limiting for transmission.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the WT Spike/ACE2 interaction is limiting for transmission and that mutations that enhance it, including the N501Y, E484K, and S477N mutations, could provide a selective advantage by increasing transmissibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and cited literature.

claim: Mutations that enhance the Spike/ACE2 interaction could provide a selective advantage by increasing transmissibility.
source: Taken together, these findings suggest that the WT Spike/ACE2 interaction is limiting for transmission and that mutations that enhance it, including the N501Y, E484K, and S477N mutations, could provide a selective advantage by increasing transmissibility.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and cited literature.

claim: A large number of RBD mutations have been identified that increase the RBD/ACE2 affinity.
source: This seems likely, given that a large number of RBD mutations have been identified that increase the RBD/ACE2 affinity (Starr et al., 2020; Zahradník et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: The appearance of E484K together with N501Y in three lineages (Alpha, Beta, and Gamma) supports the hypothesis that combinations of existing mutations may be selected because they further increase the affinity.
source: While the appearance E484K, together with N501Y in three lineages (Alpha, Beta, and Gamma), supports this, it is also possible that E484K was selected because it disrupts antibody neutraliaation, as discussed below.
evidence: This is inferred from the epidemiological patterns and experimental data.

claim: E484K may have been selected because it disrupts antibody neutralization.
source: While the appearance E484K, together with N501Y in three lineages (Alpha, Beta, and Gamma), supports this, it is also possible that E484K was selected because it disrupts antibody neutraliaation, as discussed below.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on cited literature.

claim: Studies of other enveloped viruses, including SARS-CoV, suggest that increases in affinity of viral ligands for their cellular receptors can increase cell infection and disease severity.
source: Studies of other enveloped viruses, including SARS-CoV, suggest that increases in affinity of viral ligands for their cellular receptors can increase cell infection and disease severity (Hasegawa et al., 2007; Li et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from studies of other viruses.

claim: One study found that increasing viral ligand affinity enabled the virus to infect cells with lower receptor surface density.
source: One study found that increasing this affinity enabled the virus to infect cells with lower receptor surface density (Hasegawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Increases in affinity could increase the number of host tissues infected, which could increase the severity of disease and/or increase the viral load in the upper respiratory tract, thereby increasing spread.
source: It follows that increases in affinity could increase the number of host tissues infected, which could increase the severity of disease (Cao and Li, 2020) and/or increase the viral load in the upper respiratory tract (Hoffmann et al., 2020; Wölfel et al., 2020), thereby increasing spread.
evidence: This is inferred from the data and cited literature.

claim: Neutralising antibodies present in those infected by or vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2 primarily target the RBD.
source: This is supported by the observation that neutralising antibodies present in those infected by or vaccinated against SARS-CoV-2 primarily target the RBD (Garcia-Beltran et al., 2021; Greaney et al., 2021a; Rogers et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from published literature.

claim: Two variants with RBD mutations that abrogate antibody neutralisation, Beta and Gamma, became dominant in regions with very high levels of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: Furthermore, two variants with RBD mutations that abrogate antibody neutralisation, Beta and Gamma, became dominant in regions with very high levels of prior SARS-CoV-2 infection (Cele et al., 2021; Dejnirattisai et al., 2021; Hoffmann et al., 2021; Sabino et al., 2021; Tegally et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is cited from epidemiological and immunological studies.

claim: The N501Y mutation appears to have modest effects on antibody neutralisation.
source: Both lineages include the N501Y mutation, but this appears to have modest effects on antibody neutralisation (Greaney et al., 2021a; Greaney et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is cited from immunological studies.

claim: The E484K mutation potently disrupts antibody neutralisation.
source: In contrast, the E484K mutation, also present in both variants, potently disrupts antibody neutralisation (Greaney et al., 2021a; Greaney et al., 2021b).
evidence: This is cited from immunological studies.

claim: The K417N/T mutations were selected because they facilitate immune escape.
source: Our finding that the K417N/T mutations present in Beta and Gamma variants decrease the affinity of RBD for ACE2 suggests that they were selected because they facilitate immune escape.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing decreased affinity combined with knowledge of immune escape.

claim: Mutations of K417 can block antibody neutralisation, albeit less effectively than E484K.
source: Indeed, mutations of K417 can block antibody neutralisation, albeit less effectively than E484K (Greaney et al., 2021a; Greaney et al., 2021b; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is cited from immunological studies.

claim: The affinity-reducing K417N/T mutations have only emerged together with mutations (N501Y and E484K) that increase the affinity of RBD for ACE2.
source: It is notable that these affinity-reducing K417N/T mutations have only emerged together with mutations (N501Y and E484K) that increase the affinity of RBD for ACE2, suggesting a cooperative effect between mutations that enhance immune escape and mutations that increase affinity.
evidence: This is based on epidemiological observations and the experimental data.

claim: There is a cooperative effect between mutations that enhance immune escape and mutations that increase affinity.
source: It is notable that these affinity-reducing K417N/T mutations have only emerged together with mutations (N501Y and E484K) that increase the affinity of RBD for ACE2, suggesting a cooperative effect between mutations that enhance immune escape and mutations that increase affinity.
evidence: This is inferred from the epidemiological patterns and experimental data.

claim: Carriers of the K26R and S19P ACE2 variants will be at greater risk of infection and/or severe disease.
source: The evidence summarised above that WT RBD/ACE2 binding is limiting for SARS-CoV-2 transmission, suggest that carriers of these ACE2 variants will be at greater risk of infection and/or severe disease.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the experimental data and cited literature.

claim: A preliminary analysis suggests that the carriers of the K26R ACE allele might be at increased risk of severe disease, but the findings did not reach statistical significance.
source: A preliminary analysis (MacGowan et al., 2021) suggests that the carriers of the K26R ACE allele might be at increased risk of severe disease, but the findings did not reach statistical significance, and further studies are required.
evidence: This is cited from a preliminary analysis.

claim: The RBD S477N mutation may have a selective disadvantage amongst carriers of the ACE2 S19P variant.
source: In this case, the opposite effect of the RBD S477N mutation on its affinity for ACE2 S19P (decreased), compared with ACE2 WT (increased), suggests that this RBD variant may have a selective disadvantage amongst carriers of the ACE2 S19P variant, in contrast to those with ACE2 WT, where it appears to be advantageous.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing opposite effects on affinity.

claim: The low frequency of the ACE2 S19P variant means that the selective disadvantage of RBD S477N is unlikely to be important at a population level.
source: However, the low frequency of this variant means that this is unlikely to be important at a population level and will be difficult to detect.
evidence: This is inferred from population genetics data.

claim: The two most common ACE2 variants are in positions on ACE2 with no known functional activity.
source: It is noteworthy that the two most common ACE2 variants are in positions on ACE2 with no known functional activity.
evidence: This is based on knowledge of ACE2 function.

claim: These ACE2 mutations may be a remnant of historic adaptation to pathogens that utilised this portion of ACE2.
source: This raises the question as to whether these mutations are a remnant of historic adaption to pathogens that utilised this portion of ACE2.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning.

claim: The ACE2 S19P mutation is largely confined to African/African-American populations.
source: The fact that ACE2 S19P mutation is largely confined to African/African-American populations, suggests that it is more recent than K26R and/or selected by pathogen(s) confined to the African continent.
evidence: This is based on population genetics data cited earlier.

claim: The ACE2 S19P mutation is more recent than K26R and/or selected by pathogen(s) confined to the African continent.
source: The fact that ACE2 S19P mutation is largely confined to African/African-American populations, suggests that it is more recent than K26R and/or selected by pathogen(s) confined to the African continent.
evidence: This is inferred from population genetics data.

claim: Monomeric, soluble forms of the ectodomain of ACE2 and the Spike RBD were expressed in human cells to retain native glycosylation.
source: Monomeric, soluble forms of the ectodomain of ACE2 and the Spike RBD were expressed in human cells, to retain native glycosylation, and purified (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about protein production.

claim: ACE2 was captured onto the sensor surface via a carboxy-terminal biotin.
source: ACE2 was captured onto the sensor surface via a carboxy-terminal biotin and RBD injected over ACE2 at different concentrations (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the SPR setup.

claim: Measured kon and koff rates approached maximal values at the low level of ACE2 immobilisation (~50 RU) used in the experiments.
source: The latter is demonstrated by the fact that measured kon and koff rates approached maximal values at the low level of ACE2 immobilisation (~50 RU) used in our experiments (Figure 2B,C; Dejnirattisai et al., 2021).
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2B,C.

claim: The excellent fit of the 1:1 binding model to the data excludes an effect of protein aggregates.
source: The excellent fit of the 1:1 binding model to our data excludes an effect of protein aggregates, which yield complex kinetics.
evidence: This is inferred from the quality of the fits to the data.

claim: The equilibrium KD did not vary with immobilisation level, further validating the kinetic measurements.
source: This KD was very similar to the value calculated from kinetic data (63 ± 7.7 nM [mean ± SD, n = 24, Table 1]), and did not vary with immobilisation level (Figure 2E), further validating our kinetic measurements.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the data in Figure 2E.

claim: The native Spike protein is a trimer and has several other domains, including the nearby N-terminal domain.
source: The native Spike protein is a trimer and has several other domains, including the nearby N-teminal domain, and the native ACE2 protein can exist as a dimer (Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established structural knowledge cited from literature.

claim: The native ACE2 protein can exist as a dimer.
source: The native Spike protein is a trimer and has several other domains, including the nearby N-teminal domain, and the native ACE2 protein can exist as a dimer (Yan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from structural literature.

claim: The analysis using monomeric forms of RBD and ACE2 may not detect the full effects of RBD and ACE2 mutations on the Spike/ACE2 interaction.
source: Because of these differences, our analysis may not detect the full effects of RBD and ACE2 mutations on the Spike/ACE2 interaction.
evidence: This is a caveat about the experimental system.

claim: The study has not examined the effect of these mutations on viral attachment to cells.
source: A second caveat is that we have not examined the effect of these mutations on viral attachment to cells.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the study.

claim: The affinity and kinetic data on RBD variants are broadly consistent with some recent reports.
source: Our affinity and kinetic data on RBD variants are broadly consistent with some (Laffeber et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021), but not all (Dejnirattisai et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021a), recent reports on the K417T/N, N501Y, and E484K variants.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature.

claim: The affinity and kinetic data on RBD variants are not consistent with all recent reports.
source: Our affinity and kinetic data on RBD variants are broadly consistent with some (Laffeber et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2021), but not all (Dejnirattisai et al., 2021; Zhou et al., 2021a), recent reports on the K417T/N, N501Y, and E484K variants.
evidence: This is a comparison with cited literature.
